card.t: They died to make the desert bloom.

chapters.t: The first name on the list

caps.t:
At Hoover Dam, 42 deaths were written
down as pneumonia in one of the hottest
deserts in America.

Men who worked in the tunnels said it wasn't
pneumonia at all and blamed the exhaust

from the gasoline trucks
running down there.
And because it went down as an illness,

not one of those 42 is in
the official death count.
That count says 96.

People still swear there are
men buried inside the concrete,

and there's a father and son who
both died working on this dam,

years apart, but on the
same day of the year.

So, how many people did
Hoover Dam really kill?

In the summer of 1931, the temperature
at Black Canyon went past 120 degrees,

and whole families were
living down there in tents.

America was two years
into the Great Depression,

and the government was about to build
the biggest dam anyone had tried on the
Colorado River between Nevada and Arizona.

The job went to a group of builders who
called themselves Six Companies for about 49
million dollars.
Men came looking for that work,

many of them before there
was anywhere to live,

so they camped on the river flats with
their wives and children in tents and shacks
made of whatever they could find.

People called it Ragtown, which tells you
most of what you need to know about it.

The government was building a proper
town for them up on the plateau,

Boulder City, and it would
take months to finish.
Between late June and late July,
16 people died of heat prostration,

and two of them were women who lived
there and didn't work on the dam.
None of those 16 are in the 96.

That's the first thing to know
about the official number.

The Bureau of Reclamation says its industrial
fatalities don't include deaths from
heat, pneumonia, or heart trouble.

So, a man who fell off
the canyon wall counted,

and a man who collapsed
in the heat didn't.
So, what else isn't in the 96?

The bureau's own tables are
still online year by year,
so we can count the rest ourselves.

There's a longer list
too, with 112 names on it.
That one starts years before 1931,

with the men who went looking
for a place to put the dam.

One of them was a reclamation
surveyor named John Gregory Tierney.

He was working from a
barge on the Colorado,

testing the rock for a dam site when he
went into the river in a flood and drowned.
That was the 20th of December,
and the river kept his body.
He left a son named Patrick.

Tierney's death isn't in the 96 because
that count only starts once the dam itself
was being built, years after he died.

And when it was being built, the men who
had it worst were the ones underground.

On August 7th, 1931, Six Companies moved a
group of tunnel workers to jobs that paid
less.

Within hours, the whole
work force walked out.

They put together a list, and you can hear
what the job was like in what they asked
for.
They wanted clean drinking water,
ice water in that heat, and flush toilets.

They also wanted the company
to obey the state mining laws,

and one of those laws banned
gasoline engines underground.
The company said no to all of it,

and the strikers knew
where that left them.
A quarter of the country was out of work,
so every one of them could be replaced.
They didn't hold out for long.
They did win a few things.

There were more lights
and more water on the job,

and the houses in Boulder
City went up faster.

But the pay cut stayed,
and so did the trucks.

Before they could pour a dam, they
had to move the river out of the way,

so they blasted four tunnels
through the canyon walls,
two on each side, each one 56 feet across.

Put together, they ran
for more than three miles.

Men drilled the rock face from big rigs
on the backs of trucks called jumbos,

with a whole bank of drills
hammering away at once.

Then they set the charges,
and after each blast,

the trucks came in to
haul out the broken rock.

Those trucks ran on gasoline inside the
tunnels with the engines going all day.
Nobody was opening a window down there.

Reclamation's history of the tunnels
says temperatures in there reached
140 degrees.

In November 1931, Nevada's inspector of
mines ordered Six Companies to get the
gasoline trucks out.

Six Companies went to
federal court instead.

It argued that a state law didn't fit a
federal project and that its blowers kept

the tunnel air safe, which is a strange
thing to go to court for when you think
about it.

In April 1932, the court sided with
the company for the time being,
and the trucks stayed.
By then, men were getting sick.

Between 1931 and 1935, the bureau's
tables list 42 deaths from pneumonia.

21 of them came in 1931 and 1932 while the
tunnels were being dug and in the weeks
just after.
The worst month was December 1932,
when seven Six Companies men died.
The company's doctors called it pneumonia,
but the workers had another word for it,
and that was gas.

They said it was carbon monoxide from
the truck engines and that calling it

pneumonia kept the company
clear of any blame.

Carbon monoxide poisoning was
a known danger on that job,
just like heat, thirst, and electrocution.

And this was the same exhaust Nevada had
tried to ban from the same trucks the
company had gone to court to keep.

The bureau's tables
never mention gas at all,
only pneumonia, year after year.
Now, to be fair to the company,

nobody has ever proved
it was carbon monoxide.
Pneumonia was a real killer in the 1930s,

years before there were
antibiotics to treat it,

and more than half of the 42 died after
the river was already running through those
tunnels.
So the trucks can't explain all of them.
What we can check is the bookkeeping,
and it's all in the bureau's own tables.

Pneumonia didn't count, so
whatever killed those 42 people,
the official number stayed at 96.

And there's one more story about
this dam that everybody knows,

which is that men are
buried in the concrete.

Before any concrete went in, the canyon
walls had to be cleaned off by men called
high scalers.
They hung on ropes hundreds of feet up,

knocking off loose rock
with bars and jackhammers.

Falling rock and debris killed
20 men over the whole job,

and that doesn't count the tools
and machinery that came down too.

Then came the concrete, and that's
where the legend comes from.
The dam stands

726 feet from the bedrock
to the road on top,

and there's three and a quarter
million cubic yards of concrete in it.

It gave off so much heat as it set that
they ran more than 580 miles of pipe through

it with ice water inside
just to cool it down.

With that much concrete, it's easy to
believe a man could vanish inside and nobody
would know.

But the dam went up as hundreds
of separate blocks side by side,
a bit like a giant set of building bricks.

They filled each one from buckets
that held eight cubic yards,

and the buckets came down on
cables strung across the canyon.

Every bucket raised the level by
somewhere between two and six inches,

and a crew of men called puddlers
stamped it into place with their boots.

So a man who fell in would have been lying
in a few inches of wet concrete in front
of half a dozen people.
Somebody would have noticed.
The bureau has a short answer to that one.
No one is buried in Hoover Dam.

The nearest thing happened in November
1933 when a worker named Jameson was killed

by a slide of concrete and
debris in the middle of the dam.

The bureau lists him
as killed in the slide,

not missing, and it
says nobody is in there.

On September 30th, 1935, President Franklin
Roosevelt stood on top of the finished

dam and dedicated it in front
of a crowd of thousands.

Four years earlier, this had been a river
at the bottom of a canyon with a tent camp
beside it.

The contract gave Six
Companies seven years,

and they finished the whole
job more than two years early.

But there was still work
to do on the intake towers,

the four tall concrete towers that feed
water from the lake to the turbines.

On the 20th of December 1935, a man named
Patrick Tierney fell from one of those
towers and was killed.
He was the surveyor's son.

His father is one of the first
two names on that long list,

and Patrick is the last
name in the bureau's tables.
They died on the same date, years apart.

Patrick's fall went into
the accident tables,

but his father died too
early to be in the 96.

So how many people did
Hoover Dam really kill?

In June 1934, when the
job was at its busiest,

more than 5,000 men a
day were working on it.
Over the whole job, it was about 21,000.

96 out of 21,000 sounds almost
safe for work like that,

and that's partly why the
number has lasted so long.
96 is true, but only if the question is,

how many workers died in
accidents on the site?

Add the heat deaths of 1931
and the 42 pneumonia deaths,
and you're past 150.

And that's before you count the men who
died of heart trouble or the ones who got
sick and went home to die somewhere else.

Were the pneumonia deaths
really carbon monoxide?

We can't prove it, and the
bureau's own records never say so.
But the men who breathed that air said so,

and the company fought to
keep the trucks that made it.

Our verdict is that about 150 people died
building Hoover Dam or living beside it,
not 96.

There's a plaque at the dam for
the men who died building it,

and it says, "They died
to make the desert bloom."

It was put up for the 96
men in the official count.

The 42 in the pneumonia
column aren't part of that,
and none of them are in the concrete,
whatever you've heard.

Our next story is a different
kind of American landmark,

the prison on a rock in San Francisco Bay
and the three men who might have got off
it.
